article.title: Why Calibration Can Matter More Than Ranking for Business Decisions
article.why: Understand when accurate probabilities matter more than relative ordering.

paragraphs.en:
Many predictive models are evaluated by how well they rank customers. If customers who eventually buy tend to receive higher scores than customers who do not, the model has useful discrimination. Metrics such as ROC-AUC summarize this ranking ability. But some business decisions need more than ordering. They need probabilities that mean what they claim to mean. This is the role of calibration.

Suppose a model gives 10,000 customers a predicted purchase probability near 20 percent. If the model is well calibrated, roughly 20 percent of comparable cases should actually purchase over the defined outcome window. If only 5 percent purchase, the model may still rank customers correctly, but its probability scale is misleading.

Why does that matter? Imagine a campaign costs 300 yen per customer and earns 2,000 yen of contribution margin when a purchase occurs. A decision rule based on expected value needs an estimate of purchase probability. If probabilities are systematically too high, the company may contact customers whose expected return is actually below cost. Ranking alone cannot tell the team where the economic break-even point lies.

Capacity planning provides another example. A call center may be able to contact only 50,000 customers. Ranking is essential for deciding who comes first. But if managers also want to forecast how many conversions those 50,000 contacts will produce, calibrated probabilities become important. Summing poorly calibrated scores can produce an unrealistic demand or staffing forecast.

Calibration and discrimination are separate properties. A model can rank extremely well while being poorly calibrated. It can also be reasonably calibrated but weak at separating high- and low-risk customers. Teams should therefore choose metrics according to the decision. AUC or ranking metrics help when relative ordering is the main objective. Brier score, log loss, reliability curves, calibration intercept and slope, or observed-versus-predicted plots help assess probability quality.

Calibration can drift over time even when ranking remains stable. A model trained when the natural conversion rate was 0.2 percent may continue to order customers correctly after the base rate falls to 0.1 percent, while systematically overstating absolute probabilities. Changes in eligibility, product attractiveness, economic conditions, or campaign channel can all shift the base rate.

Post-hoc calibration methods such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or other calibration models can map raw scores to better probability estimates. They should be trained on appropriate held-out or out-of-time data rather than the same observations used to fit the underlying model. Otherwise, the calibration layer can overfit.

Segment-level checks are also important. Overall calibration can look acceptable while probabilities are biased for a particular age group, company, channel, or score range. If business rules differ by segment, these errors can produce uneven allocation.

There is one more limitation: a calibrated purchase probability is still not an incremental treatment effect. It estimates what is likely to happen under the data-generating conditions represented in the target. A customer with a 30 percent purchase probability may buy without intervention. For campaign optimization, uplift or causal estimates may be needed.

The practical lesson is to ask what the score will be used for. If the business only needs a ranked list under a fixed capacity, discrimination may dominate. If it uses scores to estimate expected profit, forecast conversions, set thresholds, or compare economic scenarios, calibration becomes central. A useful probability should not merely sort customers; it should also correspond reasonably well to observed reality.

paragraphs.ja:
Ranking性能とcalibrationは別の性質です。AUCが高くても、score 0.20が実際に約20％の発生率を意味するとは限りません。expected value、break-even threshold、conversion forecast、capacity planningにscoreを使う場合、probability scaleのずれはbusiness decisionを直接誤らせます。

Brier score、log loss、reliability curve、calibration intercept/slope、observed-vs-predictedで確認できます。base rateが変わるとrankingが安定したままcalibrationだけdriftすることもあります。Platt scalingやisotonic regressionなどをheld-out/out-of-time dataで適用し、segment別にも確認します。ただしcalibrated propensityはincremental effectではないため、campaign最適化ではuplift/causal estimateが別途必要な場合があります。

vocabulary.usage: Calibration checks whether probabilities match outcomes.
A base-rate shift can hurt calibration.
Isotonic regression maps scores to probabilities.
